opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a somewhat underrated option, and I want to be careful about how I put it, because I'm not claiming it's the best thing for most people to do.

The basic argument goes like this. A lot of people think about AI risk as if what matters is what happens at the single leading company. But I think there's a decent chance the situation is messier. You might have several companies within a few months of each other, and the risk doesn't only come from whoever is in first place. If a trailing company deploys a model that's dangerously capable, maybe with weaker security or weaker safety measures, that can be really bad even if the leader is being responsible. So the safety practices at the third-, fourth-, or fifth-best company actually matter quite a lot.

The second part of the argument is about marginal impact. At a company like Anthropic, or to some extent Google DeepMind, there are already lots of people who care about catastrophic risk and are thinking hard about it. If you join, you're one more person in a fairly crowded room. At a company where there are very few people taking these risks seriously, one competent, well-informed person can matter a lot more. You might be the person who notices that model weights aren't secured well enough. You might be the person who suggests "hey, we should actually monitor what our internal coding agents are doing," or who builds a cheap control protocol that otherwise wouldn't exist. A lot of the interventions I care about, like basic AI control measures, are pretty cheap. They don't require a company to be deeply safety-focused. They just require somebody internally to push for them and make implementing them easy.

I think about this in terms of what I sometimes call the "ten people on the inside" scenario. In a world where leadership isn't very interested in safety and won't spend much on it, what can a small number of people who do care get done with a small budget? My guess is a surprisingly large fraction of the achievable risk reduction. That fraction gets much bigger if those people are there, already trusted, with context on the company's infrastructure, rather than trying to get in at the last minute.

There are real costs, of course. You might be helping a company that accelerates things. You might find you have no influence and just get absorbed. It can be pretty demoralizing to be the only person in the room who thinks this stuff matters. So I'd say it fits people who are fairly resilient, who can be pragmatic and get along with colleagues who don't share their worldview, and who are good at framing safety work in terms the company already cares about, like reliability, security, or not embarrassing ourselves. For those people I think it can be really high impact, and I'd like to see more of them do it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says few people at some companies take catastrophic risks seriously and that a small number of insiders could have impact, but does not explain why their scarcity at Meta would not reflect hostility toward them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic case here is pretty simple, which is that the thing that matters for how well the world handles transformative AI isn't just what the frontier lab does. It's what all the labs do, and in particular, it's what the labs do who are maybe a bit behind the frontier but still deploying very capable systems to a huge number of people.

So Meta's a good example. Meta is probably not going to be the first company to build a system that's dramatically smarter than humans, if I had to bet. But they're going to be building and deploying systems that are pretty capable, pretty close behind whoever's in front. And they're also doing something that the leading labs mostly aren't doing, which is releasing open-weight models. And the safety considerations there are actually quite different from the ones that come up at a lab that's keeping everything behind an API.

And my experience is that at a lot of these companies, there just aren't very many people who've thought seriously about the kinds of risks I care about — things like, what happens if the model is actually trying to undermine you? What do you do if you can't fully trust the outputs of the system you've built? Those questions are somewhat niche even at the frontier labs, and at a trailing lab, there might be basically nobody working on them. So the marginal value of one person who understands this stuff and can push for reasonable practices is plausibly pretty high. You're not the fifth person on a team of five arguing about which of two sensible policies to adopt. You might be the first person raising the question at all.

The other thing I'd say is that a lot of the work I think is most important — the control-style stuff, where you're trying to set up your deployment so that even if the model is scheming, it can't cause a catastrophe — that work has to actually be implemented at each organisation that's deploying these models. It's not like you can solve it once at one lab and the problem's solved. Every lab that's running capable models in high-stakes settings needs to have some story for why that's okay. And so if you think the number of labs that matter is more than one or two, then you want competent people at all of them.

Now, there are obvious downsides. You might have less influence than you'd hope. The company might just not care, and you might spend a lot of time being frustrated. And there's a real concern about whether your presence there is sort of laundering the company's reputation — like, "we have safety people, so it's fine" — without you actually being able to change much. I take that seriously. But I think on net, for the right kind of person — someone who's reasonably senior, who has good judgment about which battles to pick, and who's going into it clear-eyed about the fact that they might end up with little leverage — I think it's a pretty reasonable thing to do, and probably underrated by people in my community who tend to focus almost exclusively on the frontier labs.

r001.rationale: The response says few people at trailing labs have seriously considered these risks, but it does not explain whether that scarcity reflects hostility toward such people within Meta.

astra-6.text:
I think one reason is that a company can be trailing in capabilities and still become very relevant later. I wouldn’t want our strategy to depend on being confident about which companies will be at the frontier when the most dangerous systems are developed. So having people inside those companies who understand the risks, and who can help the company respond sensibly as circumstances change, seems valuable.

Another reason is that a lot of useful safety work doesn’t require having the very best model. You can work on ways of evaluating dangerous capabilities, or on techniques for controlling models that might be trying to subvert your safeguards. A trailing company might have models and infrastructure that are quite adequate for that research, and the results could be useful elsewhere.

And there’s potentially an advantage to being able to learn from the companies ahead of you. If someone else encounters a serious safety problem first, you’d like there to be people at your company who can recognise what happened and translate that into changes in what you’re doing.

I don’t think that makes any job with ‘AI safety’ in the title at Meta a good opportunity. I’d want to know what you’d actually get to work on, who would listen to the results, and whether there’s a plausible route from your work to consequential decisions. But ‘this company is currently behind’ doesn’t, by itself, seem like a strong reason to rule it out.

r001.rationale: The response argues that having people inside a trailing company understand AI risks could be valuable, but it does not address why few people concerned about existential risk are at Meta or whether that scarcity reflects hostility.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic case is that a company can be behind the frontier and still matter a lot for how AI goes. It might catch up, or it might deploy systems developed elsewhere, or its decisions about releasing models might substantially affect what everyone else can do. So there are potentially important safety decisions being made there even if it isn’t currently building the most capable model.

And being behind can give you some room to prepare. If you can see roughly what capabilities are coming, you can work on how your company should evaluate and manage those capabilities before there’s an urgent deployment decision. That could be a pretty useful position to be in.

But I’d want to evaluate the particular role. Are you going to have access to the relevant systems? Can you do useful technical work? Is there a plausible route from your work to changing a consequential decision? ‘This company does AI, and AI safety is important’ isn’t enough by itself. The value depends quite a lot on what you can actually accomplish there.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Meta’s potential influence on AI deployment and the value of preparing for capabilities, but it does not address the scarcity of people concerned about existential AI risk or whether that scarcity reflects hostility within the company.
